solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Solitude-seeker shedding old clothes

indicators.note: to shed something is to cast it off, so a letter is dropped from the name

parts.note: Greta Garbo, the film star famous for saying she wanted to be alone
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A recluse gets rid of their old outfits.
explanation.walkthrough: The solitude-seeker is Greta Garbo, whose line 'I want to be alone' made her the byword for privacy; drop the O and GARB is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Garb is a slightly formal or literary word for dress or attire, used as a collective noun just as clothes is.

clue.text: Firm fruit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' reads as an adjective describing the fruit, but it is a noun meaning a company.
explanation.definitionFit: Apple is a well-known computer and phone company and also the common round orchard fruit.

clue.text: A panda car's banged up during police round

indicators.note: what happens during something sits inside its span, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a police officer's beat is the round they patrol

indicators.note: something banged up is battered out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A police panda car gets smashed while officers are out on patrol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Panda car' looks like one phrase, the old British name for a small police patrol car, but 'A panda' is the definition and only 'car' is shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Bearcat is another name for the red panda, the small reddish tree-dwelling mammal of the Himalayas.

clue.text: Submarine controlled by steward leaving island

parts.note: to be under someone is to be controlled by them

indicators.note: when something leaves it is no longer there, so a letter departs from the word

parts.note: a steward serves food and drink, like a waiter
I is the standard abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A submarine is under the command of a ship's steward who has left an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Submarine' reads as the noun for the vessel, but here it is the adjective meaning beneath the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Submarine as an adjective means existing or happening below the surface of the sea, which is a synonym of the answer.

clue.text: College class extremely lazy to a man?

parts.note: short for university
a form is a school class

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its outer letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of lazy

explanation.surface: Is a whole college class idle, every last student?
explanation.walkthrough: A form is the usual British word for a school class or year group.
explanation.definitionFit: 'To a man' is an idiom meaning without exception, everyone alike, which is what the adverb conveys; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: Rogue sailor son punches gets shiner

indicators.note: a punch drives into something, so one piece is forced inside another

parts.note: a dog is a scoundrel, as in 'you dirty dog'
S is the standard abbreviation for son
a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: A roguish sailor's son throws a punch and ends up with a black eye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shiner' suggests a black eye from the fight; here it simply means something that shines.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dog Star is Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, so it is literally a bright shiner.

clue.text: Rubbish written about a southern cook

indicators.note: writing about something wraps around it, so one piece encloses others

parts.note: rot is nonsense
taken as written
S is the abbreviation for southern

explanation.surface: Someone writes nasty things about a cook from the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' looks like a noun for the person being criticised, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast is one particular way to cook food, in an oven with dry heat, so it is a specific example of the verb.

clue.text: An example of this would be The Thing

definitions.text: An example of this would be The
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the grammatical class that 'the' and 'a' belong to
second meaning: an object or item

explanation.walkthrough: 'The Thing' reads as a title, like the horror film, but 'The' is one example and 'Thing' is a separate meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar 'the' is the definite article, and in everyday speech an article is an object or item, a thing.

clue.text: Simple companion getting gas for SEAT

parts.note: easy means simple
CH is Companion of Honour, a British order
air is a mixture of gases

explanation.surface: A dim friend buys fuel for their SEAT car.
explanation.walkthrough: SEAT in capitals suggests the Spanish car maker, which is why the gas sounds like petrol; it is just an ordinary seat.
explanation.definitionFit: An easy chair is a large comfortable upholstered armchair, a particular kind of seat for relaxing.

clue.text: I'm a spy ranting about bug

indicators.note: a ranting person is wild and disordered, and going about stirs things round, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
the word itself is also part of the letters used

explanation.surface: A secret agent confesses while raving about a listening device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ranting' does two jobs: its letters are in the mix and it signals the shuffle along with 'about'. 'Bug' suggests a hidden microphone, fitting the spy.
explanation.definitionFit: The praying mantis is a predatory insect, and bug is an informal general word for any insect.

clue.text: Material from entry-level crossword

indicators.note: taken from means drawn out of, so the letters come straight out of the words that follow

parts.note: runs across the join of the last two words

explanation.surface: Some source material taken from an easy beginner's crossword.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters span the end of 'level' and the start of 'crossword'.
explanation.definitionFit: Velcro is the hook-and-loop fastening fabric, a trademarked textile used on shoes and bags.

clue.text: One tracks bird around about lake

indicators.note: to track is to follow behind, so the first piece comes after the next one

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
Roman numeral one
CA, circa, means around
CA, circa, also means about

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher follows a bird circling a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' and 'about' look like positional instructions, but each is simply CA, short for the Latin circa.
explanation.definitionFit: Titicaca is the large high-altitude freshwater lake on the border between Peru and Bolivia.

clue.text: I patronise general receiving award

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so one piece is put inside another

parts.note: General Custer, the US cavalry commander
OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: A general getting a medal speaks condescendingly of himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patronise' suggests talking down to someone; here it means giving a shop your business, and the clue is spoken by the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: To patronise a shop is to be a regular buyer there, so a shopper who says it describes being a paying client.

clue.text: Banal tour around foreign capital

indicators.note: turned around suggests being moved into a different order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dull sightseeing trip round a city abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tour around' reads naturally as travelling round the capital, which hides that 'around' is the rearranging signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulan Bator, also spelt Ulaanbaatar, is the capital city of Mongolia, a country outside Britain.

clue.text: European's concerning time in prison

indicators.note: being in something means being enclosed by it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: the can is slang for prison
re means concerning, as in a letter heading
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A European is worried about his spell behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's means 'is'. 'Concerning time in prison' reads like a worry about a sentence, but it lists three pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cretan is someone from Crete, the Greek island in the Mediterranean, and so a native of Europe.

clue.text: Dozy type in cap parent slapped about

indicators.note: something slapped about is knocked around roughly, so its letters end up disordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sleepy person in a hat gets cuffed by a mother or father.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is a link here, not a container signal: the definition sits in the letters that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A catnapper takes short light sleeps during the day, so is literally someone dozy or inclined to doze.

clue.text: Pretty pixie captivates ghoul ultimately

indicators.note: to captivate is literally to take captive, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: a pixie is a kind of fairy

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: last letter of ghoul

explanation.surface: A beautiful little sprite charms a monster in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty' reads as an adjective for the pixie, but it is the adverb meaning moderately, as in pretty good.
explanation.definitionFit: As adverbs both mean moderately or quite, as in 'pretty good' and 'fairly good'.

clue.text: Crashes to do with parts on cars, I'm told

parts.note: re means regarding or to do with

indicators.note: what one is told is heard rather than read, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: tyres, the British spelling of the rubber wheel covers, said out loud

explanation.surface: Someone reports on smashes involving car parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crashes' suggests car accidents, but in slang to crash is to go to sleep; British TYRES and TIRES sound identical.
explanation.definitionFit: Crash is informal for falling asleep or going to bed, and retiring is the formal term for heading off to bed.

clue.text: Civilized leader had bloody class

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of civilized
to have a meal is to eat, so had is ate
gory means bloody

explanation.surface: A cultured chief had an extremely violent classroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Civilized leader' sounds like a refined ruler, but only the first letter is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: A category is a group or division of things sharing features, which is one sense of class as a noun.

clue.text: Smoke coming from red jumper lit at the rear

parts.note: Che Guevara, the revolutionary, a red or communist
a roo, short for kangaroo, is a jumper

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its end, so only the final letter is taken

parts.note: last letter of lit

explanation.surface: Smoke rises from the back of a red sweater that has caught fire.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a jumper is a sweater, which the surface uses; here it is the kangaroo, and red is Che Guevara.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheroot is a cigar cut square at both ends, and smoke is an informal noun for anything smoked, like a cigar.

clue.text: Reason head of garrison gets ammunition

indicators.note: the head is the top, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of garrison
rounds are cartridges or shells

explanation.surface: A fort's commander is sensibly issued bullets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reason' looks like a verb, but it is the noun for a justification.
explanation.definitionFit: Grounds for something are the basis or justification for it, as in 'grounds for complaint'.

clue.text: Former pupil caught breaking old fence?

parts.note: OB, old boy, is a former pupil

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece enters another

parts.note: stale means old and no longer fresh
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: An ex-student is nabbed smashing an ancient fence.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows a fence is only one example of the answer, such as a jump in a horse race.
explanation.definitionFit: A fence in showjumping or steeplechasing is a barrier to clear, one kind of hurdle or barrier.

clue.text: One lifting swish bags close to shopper

indicators.note: to bag something is to put it in a sack, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: a cane is a stick that swishes

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is used

parts.note: last letter of shopper

explanation.surface: A shoplifter in a posh store grabs items near a customer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swish' suggests smart or posh, but here it is the noun for a whippy stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A crane is a machine that raises and moves heavy loads, so it is a thing that does the lifting.

clue.text: Coat belonging to Afghan or a Kazakh

indicators.note: what belongs to something is part of it, so the letters are found inside the words that follow

parts.note: runs across the join of the words

explanation.surface: A warm coat owned by someone from Afghanistan or Kazakhstan.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters start at the end of 'Afghan' and run into 'Kazakh'; an Afghan is also a kind of coat, a neat distraction.
explanation.definitionFit: An anorak is a hooded waterproof jacket, originally from the Arctic, so it is a type of outer garment.

clue.text: A descendent covering up king's crime

indicators.note: covering something up hides it inside, so one piece is concealed within another

parts.note: taken as written
a son is a descendant
R is the abbreviation for king, from Latin rex

explanation.surface: An heir hushes up a royal misdeed.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's means 'is', linking the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Arson is the offence of deliberately setting fire to property, a specific criminal act.

clue.text: Item of clothing soprano tarted up

indicators.note: things that are up in the air are unsettled, so the letters before this word are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A singer dresses flashily in a showy garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tarted up', British slang for made showy, looks like the anagram signal, but 'tarted' is part of the letters and 'up' alone does the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: Toreador pants are tight calf-length trousers modelled on those worn by bullfighters, a single garment.

clue.text: Gold-digger reports cop for corruption

indicators.note: corruption spoils the original form, so the letters are altered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman after money informs on a crooked police officer.
explanation.walkthrough: A gold-digger usually means someone who dates for money; here it is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A prospector searches the ground for mineral deposits such as gold, so is literally someone digging for gold.

clue.text: Number making a comeback in Salzburg on vacation?

indicators.note: to be in something is to be enclosed by it, so one piece goes inside another
vacated means emptied, so the inside letters leave and only the outer pair remain

parts.note: first and last letters of Salzburg

indicators.note: a comeback is a return journey, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: No. is the abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: A hit returns in Salzburg while the tourists are on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' does double duty as definition and as NO; Salzburg, the setting of The Sound of Music, nods to songs.
explanation.definitionFit: A number is a piece of music in a performance or on a record, so a tune or track.
